title: NEC Past Paper - Set 17 (2083 Asoj 18, 2nd shift)

questions.q: The initial setting time of ordinary Portland cement is:
questions.s: IS 269 requires at least 30 minutes before initial set, so there is time to mix, transport and place the concrete.
questions.trap: 45 minutes is the initial setting time quoted for some blended cements, and 600 minutes is the final set for OPC.
questions.trick: Initial is a floor, final is a ceiling.

questions.q: The polar moment of inertia of a hollow circular section of outer diameter D and inner diameter d is:
questions.s: The polar value J is twice the diametral value I, so π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64 becomes π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32.
questions.trap: /64 is the *diametral* moment of inertia and is the better-remembered of the two.
questions.trick: J = Ixx + Iyy = 2I for a circle, so the denominator halves.
questions.mn: 64 about a diameter, 32 about the pole.

questions.q: The arithmetic check for the rise and fall method of levelling is:
o: ΣBS − ΣFS = Σrise − Σfall = last RL − first RL
ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL + first RL
questions.s: All three quantities must give the same number; any disagreement means an arithmetic error in the booking.
questions.trap: Adding the sights instead of subtracting them gives a plausible-looking identity that checks nothing.
questions.trick: Every term in the check is a *difference*, so every sign is a minus.
questions.mn: Back minus fore, rise minus fall, last minus first.

questions.q: In the long wall-short wall method, the length of the long wall is the centre-line length plus:
o: Half the breadth at each end
The full breadth at each end
One quarter of the breadth at each end
Nothing — it equals the centre line
questions.s: The long wall runs out to the outer face at both ends, so half a breadth is added at each end; the short wall correspondingly loses half a breadth at each end.
questions.trap: Adding the full breadth double-counts the corner, which is exactly what this method exists to avoid.
questions.trick: What the long wall gains, the short wall loses — the corner is counted once.
questions.mn: Long adds half, short deducts half.

questions.q: The maximum percentage of magnesia permitted in ordinary Portland cement is:
questions.s: IS 269 limits magnesia (MgO) to 6%. In excess it hydrates long after setting and causes unsoundness.
questions.trap: Lime, silica and alumina are present in much larger proportions, which makes the small limits easy to mix up.
questions.trick: The two unsoundness limits are magnesia 6% and sulphur trioxide about 3%.

questions.q: The shrinkage limit of a soil is the water content at which:
o: Further loss of water causes no further reduction in volume
The soil starts to behave as a liquid
The soil changes from plastic to semi-solid
The soil has zero shear strength
questions.s: Below the shrinkage limit the voids no longer close as water leaves, so the volume stays constant while the soil keeps drying.
questions.trap: The plastic limit is the plastic-to-semi-solid boundary and is the neighbouring Atterberg limit.
questions.trick: It is the only limit defined by volume rather than by consistency.
questions.mn: Shrinking stops at the shrinkage limit.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT affected by a change in effective stress?
questions.s: Effective stress rearranges the grains — changing void ratio and therefore strength, compressibility and permeability. The density of the mineral grains themselves does not change.
questions.trap: "Density" suggests the bulk density of the soil, which certainly does change; the question says particle density.
questions.trick: Effective stress acts between grains; it cannot alter what a grain is made of.
questions.mn: Grains rearrange, grains do not change.

questions.q: For a site of clay with low bearing capacity, the most suitable foundation is a:
questions.s: Piles carry the load through the weak clay to a firmer stratum below, or develop it in skin friction over a long length.
questions.trap: A mat also suits weak soil by spreading the load, and is right when the weak layer is deep and uniform — piles are the general answer when capacity is low.
questions.trick: Weak soil: spread the load (raft) or go past it (piles). The weaker it is, the more you must go past it.

questions.q: The plane carrying the maximum shear stress makes what angle with the principal planes?
questions.s: The maximum shear points lie 90° from the principal points on Mohr's circle, which is 45° in the material.
questions.trap: 90° is the angle measured on the circle and is offered to catch anyone who forgets the factor of two.
questions.trick: Angles on Mohr's circle are double the real ones.
questions.mn: Halve whatever the circle tells you.

questions.q: The unsupported height of a vertical cut in clay is given by:
questions.s: The critical height Hc = 4c/γ for a pure clay with φ = 0; the tension crack accounts for half of it.
questions.trap: 2c/γ is the depth of the tension crack alone — exactly half the critical height, and the commonest wrong answer.
questions.trick: Tension crack 2c/γ, unsupported cut twice that.

questions.q: The head loss due to sudden expansion in a pipe is:
questions.s: Applying momentum and energy across the expansion leaves the loss as the velocity head of the *difference* in velocities.
questions.trap: Writing the sum instead of the difference gives a loss even when nothing changes, which cannot be right.
questions.trick: If V1 = V2 there is no expansion and the loss must vanish — only the difference form does that.

questions.q: When a shear stress is applied to a fluid, the fluid undergoes:
questions.s: That is the definition of a fluid: it cannot sustain a shear stress at rest and keeps deforming for as long as the stress is applied.
questions.trap: A solid gives a finite deformation and then stops, which is the picture most candidates carry from strength of materials.
questions.trick: Ask whether it ever stops moving — a solid does, a fluid does not.

questions.q: If the sequent depth ratio in a hydraulic jump is 5, the jump formed is:
questions.s: A ratio of about 5 corresponds to a Froude number of roughly 4.5-9, which is the steady jump — well-defined and the best energy dissipator.
questions.trap: "Strong" sounds like the most vigorous and so the one with the largest ratio; strong jumps need Fr above about 9.
questions.trick: Steady is the design jump — stilling basins aim at it.

questions.q: The power of a centrifugal pump is directly proportional to:
questions.s: By the affinity laws head varies as D² and discharge as D³, so power — their product — varies as D⁵ at constant speed.
questions.trap: D³ is the discharge relation and is the most quoted of the affinity laws.
questions.trick: Multiply the head law by the discharge law to get the power law.

questions.q: Flow in a uniformly tapering pipe carrying a constant discharge is:
questions.s: Constant discharge makes it steady in time; the changing cross-section makes the velocity change along the pipe, so it is non-uniform in space.
questions.trap: "Constant discharge" suggests uniform flow, but uniformity is about position, not time.
questions.trick: Steady = no change with time. Uniform = no change with distance.

questions.q: The velocity of a pressure wave in water hammer depends mainly on:
o: The bulk modulus and density of the fluid and the pipe elasticity
The velocity of the flow and the length of the pipeline alone
The time taken to close the valve and the operator who closes it
The roughness of the pipe wall and the number of bends in the line
questions.s: C = √(K/ρ) for a rigid pipe, reduced when the pipe wall can stretch. For water in a rigid pipe this is about 1440 m/s.
questions.trap: Valve closure time decides whether the closure is rapid or slow, and so the *pressure rise* — but not the wave speed.
questions.trick: Wave speed is a property of the medium, not of what you do to it.
questions.mn: Wave speed C = √(K/ρ), about 1440 m/s in water.

questions.q: With a water application efficiency of 80% and a conveyance loss of 20%, the water required at the outlet to store 5 cm at the root zone is:
questions.s: Divide by both efficiencies in turn: 5/0.8 = 6.25 cm at the field, then 6.25/0.8 = 7.81 cm at the outlet (a 20% conveyance loss leaves 80%).
questions.trap: 6.25 cm applies only the application efficiency — the single most common half-finished answer.
questions.trick: Work backwards from the root zone, dividing once for each loss.

questions.q: Compared with a balanced section, the depth of the neutral axis in an under-reinforced section is:
questions.s: With less steel, less compression is needed to balance the tension, so the neutral axis rises. The steel yields before the concrete crushes, which gives a ductile warning.
questions.trap: Over-reinforced sections have a *deeper* neutral axis, and the two cases are easily swapped.
questions.trick: Less steel → less compressive force needed → smaller compression block.

questions.q: A simply supported beam has equal overhangs carrying equal point loads at both ends. The bending moment between the supports is:
questions.s: Between the supports there is no shear, and a zero shear force means a constant bending moment — the classic pure-bending arrangement.
questions.trap: "Maximum at mid-span" is true for almost every other loading, so it is the habitual answer.
questions.trick: dM/dx = V; zero shear means the moment cannot change.
questions.mn: No shear, no change in moment.

questions.q: The deflection at the centre of a simply supported beam carrying a central point load P is:
questions.s: The standard case: PL³/48EI, the largest of the simply supported deflections for a given load.
questions.trap: PL³/192EI is the same load on a *fixed* beam — four times stiffer.
questions.trick: Simple 48, fixed 192 — a factor of four for the fixity.

questions.q: The strain energy stored in a cantilever of length L carrying a point load P at its free end, due to bending alone, is:
questions.s: U = ∫M²dx/2EI with M = Px gives P²L³/6EI.
questions.trap: All four options share P²L³/EI and differ only in the denominator, so the integration must actually be done.
questions.trick: Integrating x² over the length brings the 3 in the denominator, and 2EI brings the other factor of 2.

questions.q: A three-hinged arch is:
questions.s: Four reaction components with three equations of equilibrium plus the condition that the moment at the crown hinge is zero — four equations, four unknowns.
questions.trap: A two-hinged arch is indeterminate to degree one, and the two are constantly swapped.
questions.trick: Each extra hinge removes one redundancy; three hinges make it determinate.
questions.mn: Three hinges, three equations plus one.

questions.q: Shear reinforcement in a beam is provided to resist:
o: Inclined (diagonal tension) cracks starting near the supports
Shrinkage cracks on the top surface
Cracks caused by corrosion of the main steel
questions.s: Shear is greatest at the supports, where the principal tension acts at about 45° and opens a diagonal crack. Stirrups cross that crack.
questions.trap: Vertical cracks at mid-span are flexural and are resisted by the main longitudinal steel.
questions.trick: Shear is maximum where the moment is minimum — at the supports.

questions.q: The maximum energy a material can absorb without undergoing permanent deformation is called:
questions.s: Proof resilience is the strain energy stored up to the elastic limit. Divided by the volume it becomes the modulus of resilience.
questions.trap: The modulus of resilience is the same quantity *per unit volume* — a true statement about a different quantity.
questions.trick: Proof resilience is total; modulus of resilience is per volume.
questions.mn: Proof = whole body, modulus = per unit.

questions.q: Which of the following can be obtained directly from the flexure equation M/I = σ/y = E/R?
o: The bending stress at any depth
The depth of the neutral axis
questions.s: Given M, I and y the equation returns σ at once. The neutral axis position is needed *before* I can be computed, and shear and deflection need other relations.
questions.trap: "Depth of neutral axis" is tempting because the equation is written about that axis — but it is an input, not an output.
questions.trick: Ask what each symbol in the equation already assumes you know.
questions.mn: Flexure gives stress, not shear and not deflection.

questions.q: In moment distribution, the distribution factor for a member at a joint is:
o: The stiffness of that member divided by the total stiffness at the joint
The moment in that member divided by the total applied moment
The length of that member divided by the total length
The inertia of that member divided by the total inertia
questions.s: The unbalanced moment is shared in proportion to stiffness k = I/L, so DF = k/Σk.
questions.trap: "Moment carried divided by total moment" is the *result* of applying the factor, offered as if it were the definition.
questions.trick: The factor must be computable before any moment is known.
questions.mn: Distribution factor = k/Σk, stiffness over total stiffness.

questions.q: The grade of concrete generally used for a damp-proof course at plinth level is:
questions.s: A 1:2:4 (M15) mix, usually 75 mm thick with a waterproofing compound, is the standard DPC at plinth level.
questions.trap: M20 is the minimum for reinforced work, which makes it the reflex answer for any concrete question.
questions.trick: A DPC is plain concrete, so the grade is below the RCC minimum.

questions.q: The Indian Standard code for general construction in steel is:
questions.s: IS 800 is the code of practice for general construction in steel; IS 456 is for plain and reinforced concrete.
questions.trap: IS 875 and IS 1893 are also steel-relevant — they give the loads, not the design of the steelwork.
questions.trick: 800 for steel, 456 for concrete, 875 for loads, 1893 for earthquake.
questions.mn: IS 800 steel, IS 456 concrete, IS 875 loads.

questions.q: The Indian Standard code that gives dead loads on buildings is:
questions.s: IS 875 is in five parts: Part 1 dead loads, Part 2 imposed loads, Part 3 wind, Part 4 snow and Part 5 combinations.
questions.trap: Part 2 (imposed loads) is used far more often in design and is the one most candidates recall.
questions.trick: The parts run in the order the loads are applied: dead first.

questions.q: The consistency of cement is determined by:
questions.s: The Vicat apparatus with a 10 mm plunger gives the standard consistency; the same apparatus with different needles gives the setting times.
questions.trap: Le Chatelier is also a cement test — for soundness, not consistency.
questions.trick: Vicat does consistency and both setting times; Le Chatelier does soundness.

questions.q: A high-strength friction-grip bolt is designed primarily for:
questions.s: Pre-tensioning clamps the plies together and the load is carried by friction at the faying surfaces before the bolt shank is ever engaged.
questions.trap: Ordinary bolts are designed for shear and bearing, and that calculation is the one practised most.
questions.trick: The name states the mechanism.

questions.q: Euler's buckling load for a column with both ends hinged is:
questions.s: The effective length equals the actual length for pinned ends, so the formula takes its basic form.
questions.trap: 4π²EI/L² is the both-ends-fixed case, four times stronger.
questions.trick: Hinged-hinged is the reference case with multiplier 1.

questions.q: Which distribution system suits a town that has grown outwards from a central point?
questions.s: The town is divided into zones, each with a central tank from which mains radiate outwards — fast, high-pressure delivery with simple calculation.
questions.trap: The ring system also suits a well-planned town; it surrounds rather than radiates.
questions.trick: Radial means from the centre outwards, like spokes.

questions.q: Compared with a conservancy system, the water carriage system needs:
o: A much larger quantity of water
questions.s: Sewage is carried away in flowing water, so a large and dependable supply is essential; that is why the system fails where water is scarce.
questions.trap: It does reduce manual handling and that is its main advantage — the question asks what it *needs*, not what it gives.
questions.trick: Water carriage carries waste with water, so water is the requirement.

questions.q: Manhole covers are normally made of:
questions.s: Cast iron resists the corrosive sewer atmosphere and carries wheel loads in compression, where it is strong.
questions.trap: Mild steel is stronger in tension and is the general structural choice, but it corrodes quickly over a sewer.
questions.trick: The cover sits in a wet, corrosive, compression-only duty — exactly cast iron's niche.
questions.mn: Sewers eat steel; cast iron survives.

questions.q: The saturation dissolved oxygen content of water at standard conditions is about:
questions.s: At 20 °C and one atmosphere, water holds about 9.08 mg/l of dissolved oxygen; the value falls as temperature rises.
questions.trap: 14.6 mg/l is the saturation value at 0 °C and 4 mg/l is the minimum needed to keep fish alive.
questions.trick: Cold water holds more oxygen — 14.6 at freezing, about 9 at room temperature.

questions.q: The permissible concentration of arsenic in drinking water in Nepal is:
questions.s: The Nepal National Drinking Water Quality Standard sets arsenic at 0.05 mg/l; the WHO guideline is the stricter 0.01 mg/l.
questions.trap: 0.01 mg/l is quoted by almost every international text, and it is the WHO figure rather than the Nepali one.
questions.trick: Nepal's standard is five times the WHO guideline for arsenic.

questions.q: The rate of filtration in a rapid sand filter is about:
questions.s: Rapid sand filters operate at roughly 3-6 cubic metres per square metre per hour, some thirty times the slow sand filter rate.
questions.trap: 0.1-0.2 m³/m²/hour is the slow sand filter rate, and the two rates are the classic pairing.
questions.trick: Rapid is about thirty times slow.

questions.q: A canal drop is provided when:
o: The ground slope is steeper than the designed canal bed slope
The ground slope is flatter than the canal bed slope
The canal crosses a drainage line
questions.s: Steeper ground means surplus height to be lost; it is taken out in a vertical drop rather than in continuous steep (and scouring) canal slope.
questions.trap: A canal crossing a drainage line calls for an aqueduct or a super-passage, not a drop.
questions.trick: Surplus fall must be shed somewhere.

questions.q: When lateral sub-surface drainage is provided in one direction only and longitudinal drains collect the water, the road also requires:
questions.s: An intercepting drain cuts off the seepage arriving from the uphill side before it reaches the pavement structure.
questions.trap: Extra surface drainage sounds like the complementary measure, but the problem described is sub-surface flow.
questions.trick: Water coming from one side must be intercepted on that side.
questions.mn: Cut it off before it arrives.

questions.q: The usual depth of a facultative oxidation (stabilisation) pond is:
questions.s: About a metre to a metre and a half keeps the upper layer aerobic through algal photosynthesis while the bottom stays anaerobic.
questions.trap: A deeper pond would store more, but light would not reach far enough to keep the top aerobic.
questions.trick: The depth is set by how far sunlight penetrates.

questions.q: A risk that arises outside the project but can significantly affect its scope is called:
questions.s: Contextual (external) risk comes from the political, legal, social or environmental setting and is outside the project's control.
questions.trap: Strategic risk is also "big picture" but concerns the organisation's own choices rather than its surroundings.
questions.trick: Context = the world around the project.

questions.q: The first step in the environmental impact assessment process in Nepal is:
questions.s: Scoping identifies the significant issues to be studied; the terms of reference are then written from the scoping document and approved.
questions.trap: The terms of reference are approved first by the ministry, so they feel like the beginning — but they are drafted from the scoping result.
questions.trick: You cannot write terms of reference until you know what is in scope.

questions.q: The distribution main of a water supply system is designed for:
questions.s: Distribution mains must cope with the peak hour; the pumping main and treatment works are sized on the maximum daily demand.
questions.trap: Maximum daily demand is the design figure for almost every other component, so it is the habitual answer.
questions.trick: The nearer to the tap, the shorter the peak that matters.
questions.mn: Mains for the hour, works for the day.

questions.q: Which of the following is an organic insulating material?
questions.s: Wood pulp comes from a living source and so is organic; asbestos, glass wool and mineral wool are all mineral in origin.
questions.trap: All four insulate well, so the question turns entirely on the word "organic".
questions.trick: Organic means it once grew.
questions.mn: If it grew, it is organic.

questions.q: The chemical formula of bleaching powder is:
questions.s: Calcium oxychloride, CaOCl₂, carries about 30-35% available chlorine when fresh.
questions.trap: CaCl₂ differs by a single oxygen and is a completely different compound with no disinfecting power.
questions.trick: Bleaching needs oxygen and chlorine together.
questions.mn: Ca-O-Cl₂: the O is the whole point.

questions.q: The sensitivity of a clay is:
o: Undisturbed strength divided by remoulded strength
Remoulded strength divided by undisturbed strength
The difference between the two strengths
questions.s: Remoulding destroys the structure, so the undisturbed strength is the larger; sensitivity is therefore at least 1.
questions.trap: Inverting the ratio gives a number less than one, which no sensitivity classification uses.
questions.trick: Sensitivity must be ≥ 1, so the bigger strength goes on top.

questions.q: Which canal is preferred when the cultivable command area lies on one side only?
questions.s: A contour canal runs along a contour with the land falling away on one side, so it can irrigate on that side only.
questions.trap: A ridge (watershed) canal runs along the ridge line and commands land on *both* sides — the opposite case.
questions.trick: On a ridge you can irrigate both ways; on a hillside only downhill.
questions.mn: Ridge = both sides, contour = one side.

questions.q: The structure provided to discharge surplus water out of a canal is a:
questions.s: An escape disposes of excess water into a natural drain, protecting the canal banks from overtopping.
questions.trap: A canal inlet does exactly the reverse — it admits drainage water into the canal.
questions.trick: Escape lets water escape.

questions.q: Which statement about bearing capacity theories is correct?
o: Meyerhof's theory is applicable to deep foundations
Terzaghi's theory is applicable to deep foundations
Skempton's theory applies to cohesionless soil
Terzaghi's theory ignores the depth of the footing
questions.s: Meyerhof extended bearing capacity analysis to deep foundations by including the shear strength of the soil above the base. Terzaghi's theory is for shallow footings and Skempton's for saturated clay.
questions.trap: Terzaghi is the best-known name, so it is attached to whatever the question asks about.
questions.trick: Terzaghi shallow, Meyerhof deep, Skempton clay.

questions.q: The major difference between a weir and a barrage is that a barrage:
o: Raises the water level mainly by gates rather than by a raised crest
Is built of masonry while a weir is always built of concrete
Cannot pass a flood and must be bypassed during the monsoon
Needs no head regulator because the canal draws directly from it
questions.s: A barrage has a low crest and large gates, so the level is controlled by gate operation; a weir raises the level with its crest and has little gated capacity.
questions.trap: Both structures divert water and both have head regulators, so the distinction must be found in how the afflux is created.
questions.trick: Gates mean control; a crest means no control.

questions.q: In a weir founded on a pervious foundation, the uplift pressure is a maximum at the:
o: Junction of the pile and the concrete base
questions.s: Seepage enters upstream at full head and loses head as it travels, so the residual uplift is greatest where it enters.
questions.trap: The exit gradient is critical at the *downstream* end, which makes that end feel like the dangerous one — it is, for piping, not for uplift.
questions.trick: Uplift follows the head, and the head is highest where the seepage starts.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a river training structure?
questions.s: A contour bund is a soil conservation measure on agricultural land. Spurs, guide bunds and launching aprons all train a river.
questions.trap: A contour bund is an earthwork that controls water, so it belongs to the same general family — just not to rivers.
questions.trick: Ask whether it is built in or beside a river channel.
questions.mn: Contour bund farms, the rest train rivers.

questions.q: An impermeable spur:
o: Attracts, repels or deflects the current to control erosion
Allows flow through it to reduce velocity
Is built of loose boulders only
questions.s: A solid (impermeable) spur deflects the current away from the bank; depending on its orientation it is classed as attracting, repelling or deflecting.
questions.trap: Allowing flow through to reduce velocity is what a *permeable* spur does — the exact opposite construction.
questions.trick: Impermeable means the water must go round it.

questions.q: Pharping (1911) was Nepal's first hydropower plant. Sundarijal followed after about:
questions.s: Sundarijal was commissioned in 1934, twenty-two years after Pharping.
questions.trap: The round number 20 is the natural guess and is offered immediately beside the correct one.
questions.trick: 1911 and 1934 — subtract rather than estimate.

questions.q: The recommended top width of a low earthen dam of height H is:
questions.s: The empirical rule gives a top width of 0.2H + 3 metres, with a practical minimum for access of about 3 m.
questions.trap: The other coefficients produce reasonable-looking widths for a typical height, so the formula must actually be remembered.
questions.trick: Even at zero height the rule leaves 3 m — the width of a vehicle track.
questions.mn: One-fifth of the height, plus three.

questions.q: The live storage of a reservoir is the volume between:
o: The minimum pool level and the full reservoir level
The maximum and the minimum pool levels
The minimum pool level and the bed level
The full reservoir level and the maximum water level
questions.s: Live (useful) storage lies between the lowest level from which water can be drawn and full reservoir level. Below the minimum pool level is dead storage.
questions.trap: Between full reservoir level and maximum water level is the *surcharge* storage, used only during floods.
questions.trick: Dead below, live in the middle, surcharge on top.
questions.mn: Live storage is what you can actually use.

questions.q: Which type of earthen embankment dam is suited to an impervious foundation?
questions.s: If the foundation itself stops seepage, a single material throughout is sufficient and cheapest; zoned and diaphragm sections exist to control seepage.
questions.trap: A zoned dam with a clay core looks like the "best" dam, so it is picked when the question is really about economy.
questions.trick: If the ground is already impervious, there is nothing for a core to do.

questions.q: When the reduced level increases along the length of a road, the gradient is:
questions.s: An increase in reduced level means the road is climbing, which is a rising or positive gradient.
questions.trap: "Ruling gradient" is a design limit rather than a direction, and is the best-known term in the chapter.
questions.trick: Reduced level is height, so rising level means rising road.

questions.q: The angle measured where two gradients meet at a vertical intersection is the:
questions.s: The deviation angle is the algebraic difference between the two grades and governs the length of the vertical curve.
questions.trap: The deflection angle is the equivalent quantity in *horizontal* curves, and the two are routinely swapped.
questions.trick: Deflection turns left or right; deviation goes up or down.
questions.mn: Deviation for vertical, deflection for horizontal.

questions.q: As recommended by the Department of Roads, the CBR value for a design traffic above 20 million ESAL is taken at the:
questions.s: Heavier traffic demands a more conservative subgrade value, so the 98th percentile is used above 20 msa.
questions.trap: The 90th percentile applies to intermediate traffic and the 85th to light traffic, so all three appear credible.
questions.trick: The heavier the traffic, the higher the percentile.

questions.q: The impact value of a road aggregate is determined by:
questions.s: A 13.5 kg hammer is dropped fifteen times through 380 mm, and the impact value is the percentage of fines produced.
questions.trap: The Los Angeles abrasion test also measures toughness, but by abrasion in a rotating drum rather than by impact.
questions.trick: Impact value comes from the impact test — the resistance measured is to sudden shock.

questions.q: The number of vehicles passing a section of road per unit time is called the traffic:
questions.s: Volume is the count actually observed; capacity is the maximum the road could carry under given conditions.
questions.trap: Capacity is also expressed in vehicles per hour, so the units do not distinguish them.
questions.trick: Volume is what happens, capacity is what could happen.
questions.mn: Count it and it is volume.

questions.q: Tie bars in a rigid pavement are provided:
o: Across longitudinal joints to hold the slabs together
Across transverse joints to transfer load
At the pavement edge to prevent settlement
Under the slab to resist uplift
questions.s: Tie bars are deformed bars that hold adjacent lanes in contact across a longitudinal joint. They are not designed to transfer wheel load.
questions.trap: Dowel bars do the load transfer, at transverse joints, and are plain and greased so they can slide.
questions.trick: Tie bars tie; dowel bars transfer.

questions.q: Isometric projection is a type of:
questions.s: Axonometric projection covers isometric, dimetric and trimetric, in which the object is rotated so that three faces show in one view.
questions.trap: Oblique projection also shows three faces, but it keeps one face true and projects the depth at an angle.
questions.trick: Isometric is the special axonometric case where all three axes are equally foreshortened.
questions.mn: Iso = equal, and it is axonometric.

questions.q: The Nepal Engineering Council Act was enacted in:
questions.s: The NEC Act 2055 established the Council to register engineers and regulate the profession.
questions.trap: 2056 is the year of the NEC Regulation, made under the Act, so the two dates sit one apart.
questions.trick: Act 2055, Regulation 2056.
questions.mn: Act first, rules the year after.

questions.q: In resource smoothing, the binding constraint is:
questions.s: Smoothing keeps the completion date fixed and uses float to even out the resource histogram. Levelling does the reverse — it fixes the resource limit and lets the duration stretch.
questions.trap: Resource levelling is the better-known technique and has exactly the opposite constraint.
questions.trick: Smoothing smooths within the time you have.
questions.mn: Smooth the resources, keep the date.

questions.q: In procurement, QCBS stands for:
questions.s: QCBS scores technical quality and price together, usually weighting quality around 80% for consultancy services.
questions.trap: "Quantity" differs from "quality" by two letters and reads plausibly in a procurement context.
questions.trick: The method balances how good against how much.

questions.q: The primary force responsible for the settling of particles in a sedimentation tank is:
questions.s: Particles settle because they are denser than water; Stokes' law balances the gravitational force against drag and buoyancy.
questions.trap: Buoyancy and drag both act, but they *oppose* settling — gravity is what drives it.
questions.trick: Remove gravity and nothing settles.

questions.q: An object weighs 5 kN in air and 2 kN when immersed in water. The upthrust is:
questions.s: The apparent loss of weight is the buoyant force: 5 − 2 = 3 kN, equal to the weight of water displaced.
questions.trap: 2 kN is the weight *in* water, and is what the question hands you rather than what it asks for.
questions.trick: Upthrust is always the difference between the two weights.
questions.mn: Loss of weight is the upthrust.

questions.q: The band of concrete provided below a window frame in a masonry building is called a:
questions.s: The sill band runs at window sill level and controls the cracking that starts at the lower corners of openings in an earthquake.
questions.trap: The lintel band is the better-known of the two and sits directly *above* the opening.
questions.trick: Sill below, lintel above.

questions.q: Which of the following is a negative impact of technology on society?
questions.s: Technological development consumes resources and produces waste and emissions; the other three are benefits.
questions.trap: Replacement of labour by machines is also offered in some versions and is genuinely double-edged; environmental damage is unambiguously negative.
questions.trick: Pick the one nobody would list as a benefit.

questions.q: Grouting can be used to stabilise all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.s: Grout fills voids, fissures and pores. Sound rock has none to fill, so there is nothing for the grout to do.
questions.trap: Rock appears twice in the options, once sound and once fissured, and only one of them needs treating.
questions.trick: No voids, no grouting.
questions.mn: Grout fills gaps; hard rock has none.

questions.q: The centre of gravity of a solid sphere lies at a distance from every point on its surface of:
questions.s: The centre of gravity is at the geometric centre, which is one radius — that is, D/2 — from every surface point.
questions.trap: 3R/8 is the centre of gravity of a *hemisphere* and is the figure drilled in most revision notes.
questions.trick: A full sphere is symmetrical, so its centroid can only be at the centre.

questions.q: The Kulekhani storage hydropower project was constructed with assistance from:
questions.s: Kulekhani I and II were built with Japanese assistance together with the World Bank and other partners.
questions.trap: India and China have financed many Nepali schemes, which makes both plausible for any such question.
questions.trick: Kulekhani is the Japanese-assisted storage project.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of a diversion headworks?
questions.s: An aqueduct is a cross-drainage work that carries a canal over a natural drain, well away from the headworks.
questions.trap: All four are irrigation structures, so the question turns on where each one stands.
questions.trick: The headworks sits on the river; the aqueduct sits on the canal.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a river training work?
questions.s: A canal bund retains water in a canal. Marginal bunds, guide bunds and launching aprons all control a river.
questions.trap: "Canal bund" and "guide bund" share the word bund, and both are embankments.
questions.trick: Training works act on a river, not on a canal.
questions.mn: Canal bund belongs to the canal.

questions.q: At a turning point in levelling, which readings are taken?
o: Both a fore sight and a back sight
questions.s: The fore sight is taken before the instrument is moved and the back sight after it is set up again, so the turning point carries both.
questions.trap: A change point feels like an ordinary station where one reading would do; it is the only point with two.
questions.trick: The turning point is the link between two instrument positions, so it must be read from both.

questions.q: The unconfined compression test gives:
o: The undrained shear strength of clay
The drained shear strength of sand
questions.s: With no confining pressure and no drainage, cu = qu/2 for a saturated clay. The test cannot be performed on sand, which will not stand unsupported.
questions.trap: The triaxial test also gives undrained strength, which makes the distinguishing feature the *unconfined* condition.
questions.trick: No cell pressure means no friction can be mobilised, so only cohesion is measured.
questions.mn: Unconfined: cu = qu/2, cohesion only, φ = 0.

questions.q: In a standard Proctor test, the maximum dry density occurs at:
questions.s: Below the optimum there is not enough water to lubricate the grains; above it, water occupies space the solids could have filled.
questions.trap: The Atterberg limits are also water contents, which makes any of them a plausible-looking answer.
questions.trick: The compaction curve has one peak, and the water content at that peak is what it is named for.

questions.q: Which geological formation both stores and transmits water in significant quantity?
questions.s: An aquifer is both porous and permeable. An aquiclude stores but will not transmit, an aquitard transmits slowly and an aquifuge does neither.
questions.trap: An aquiclude also holds water, which is half the requirement — the question asks for both properties.
questions.trick: Storage needs porosity; transmission needs permeability. Only one formation has both.
questions.mn: Aquifer gives water; the rest keep it.

questions.q: The minimum grade of concrete for reinforced work under normal exposure as per IS 456 is:
questions.s: IS 456 requires M20 as the minimum for reinforced concrete in mild exposure; higher grades are required as exposure worsens.
questions.trap: M15 is the minimum for *plain* concrete and is the figure attached to the lean mixes used in blinding and DPC.
questions.trick: Plain M15, reinforced M20.

questions.q: The specific speed of a Pelton wheel with a single jet is of the order of:
questions.s: A single-jet Pelton has the lowest specific speed of all turbines; Francis runs about 60-300 and Kaplan above 300.
questions.trap: Adding jets raises the specific speed, so a multi-jet Pelton reaches 30-50 and blurs the boundary.
questions.trick: High head goes with low specific speed.

questions.q: The road pattern in which roads radiate from a centre and are joined by concentric rings is the:
questions.s: Radial roads carry traffic to and from the centre and the rings distribute it without passing through the middle.
questions.trap: The grid iron pattern is the best-known layout and is the default answer for any road pattern question.
questions.trick: Radiating lines plus rings is exactly what the name describes.

questions.q: A hyetograph is a plot of:
questions.s: A hyetograph shows how the intensity of a storm varies through its duration; the hydrograph is the corresponding plot of runoff.
questions.trap: The hydrograph differs by two letters and is the far commoner term.
questions.trick: Hyeto- is rain, hydro- is water in the channel.

questions.q: In a masonry wall, the vertical joints in successive courses should be:
o: Twice as thick as the bed joints
questions.s: Breaking the vertical joints spreads the load across the wall; continuous vertical joints create a plane of weakness the wall can split along.
questions.trap: Aligned joints look neater and are easier to lay, which is why the rule has to be taught.
questions.trick: A continuous vertical joint is a ready-made crack.
questions.mn: Break the joint, bond the wall.

questions.q: In a determinate truss, the member forces are found by the method of:
questions.s: Equilibrium alone is enough for a determinate truss, so the method of joints and the method of sections both suffice.
questions.trap: Moment distribution, slope deflection and the three-moment equation are all methods for *indeterminate* structures.
questions.trick: Determinate means equilibrium is sufficient — no compatibility needed.

questions.q: The sludge returned to the aeration tank in the conventional activated sludge process is about:
questions.s: Returning roughly a quarter to a half of the flow maintains the concentration of micro-organisms needed to treat the incoming sewage.
questions.trap: Extended aeration uses much higher return ratios, which makes the larger figures look defensible.
questions.trick: The return keeps the biomass up; it is a fraction of the flow, not a multiple.
questions.mn: Conventional return: a quarter to a half.

questions.q: The ruling gradient for a road in plain terrain as per Nepal Road Standard is about:
questions.s: The ruling (design) gradient in plain and rolling terrain is around 3.3% (1 in 30); mountainous terrain allows considerably steeper.
questions.trap: 7% is the limiting gradient in hilly terrain and is the figure most often memorised.
questions.trick: Flat ground gets the gentlest gradient.
questions.mn: Plain terrain 1 in 30 (3.3%); hilly far steeper.

questions.q: The time at which the present worth of a project's benefits equals the present worth of its costs is the:
questions.s: The payback period is the time taken for cumulative returns to recover the investment; a shorter payback means a quicker return of capital.
questions.trap: Economic life is when the asset should be replaced, which is a different question about the same cash flows.
questions.trick: Payback asks when you get your money back.

questions.q: The timber defect caused by a separation of the annual rings from one another is called:
questions.s: A cup shake is a curved split that follows an annual ring; heart and star shakes run radially from the centre.
questions.trap: All three "shakes" are splits in the same log, differing only in direction.
questions.trick: A cup is curved, like the ring it follows.
questions.mn: Cup follows the ring, star and heart cross it.

questions.q: The continuity equation for steady incompressible flow in a pipe is:
questions.s: The volume passing each section per second must be the same, so the product of area and velocity is constant.
questions.trap: For compressible flow the densities enter as ρ1A1V1 = ρ2A2V2; dropping them is valid only when the density is constant.
questions.trick: Narrow the pipe and the water must speed up, so area and velocity are inversely related.

questions.q: The clear cover to the main reinforcement in a slab under mild exposure is generally:
questions.s: IS 456 gives 20 mm nominal cover for a slab in mild exposure; beams take 25 mm, columns 40 mm and footings 50 mm.
questions.trap: 15 mm is the cover for a slab with bars of 12 mm or less in very mild conditions, and is the lower figure quoted in some tables.
questions.trick: Cover increases as the member gets closer to the ground: slab, beam, column, footing.
questions.mn: Cover: slab 20, beam 25, column 40, footing 50 mm.

questions.q: A foundation is classed as shallow when:
o: The depth is not greater than the width
The depth is at least four times the width
The width is at least four times the depth
questions.s: Terzaghi's classification takes Df ≤ B as shallow, so that the shear strength of the soil above the base can reasonably be ignored.
questions.trap: The ratio is easy to invert, and "D/B > 4" is offered as the definition of a *deep* foundation.
questions.trick: Shallow means not deep: the depth must be the smaller dimension.

questions.q: The function of a forebay in a run-of-river scheme is to:
o: Act as a small balancing reservoir before the penstock
Dissipate the energy of the flow
Trap bed load from the river
Regulate the river level at the intake
questions.s: The forebay stores a small volume to absorb short-term fluctuations in demand and keeps the penstock supplied at a steady level.
questions.trap: A settling basin traps sediment and sits just upstream of the forebay, so the two are easily confused.
questions.trick: The forebay is the last pond before the pressure pipe.
questions.mn: Fore-bay: the bay before the penstock.

questions.q: The float of an activity that lies on the critical path is:
questions.s: The critical path is the longest path through the network; any delay on it delays the project, which is exactly what zero float means.
questions.trap: "Always positive" is true of every *non*-critical activity, which is the larger group.
questions.trick: If it had float, it would not be critical.

questions.q: The daily traffic averaged over a 30-day survey within a year is reported as:
questions.s: Only a count covering the full 365 days can be called the annual average; anything shorter is simply average daily traffic.
questions.trap: AADT is the term used in design and so is the one that comes to mind first.
questions.trick: The first A in AADT demands a whole year.
questions.mn: No full year, no second A.

questions.q: The hardness of water is chiefly caused by:
questions.s: Calcium and magnesium bicarbonates give temporary hardness; their sulphates and chlorides give permanent hardness.
questions.trap: Iron and manganese cause staining and taste but not hardness.
questions.trick: Hardness is measured as calcium carbonate, which names the culprit.
questions.mn: Ca and Mg make it hard.

questions.q: The point in a beam where the bending moment changes sign is called the point of:
questions.s: At a point of contraflexure the moment passes through zero and the curvature reverses; no reinforcement is needed for moment there.
questions.trap: The point of zero *shear* is where the moment is a maximum — the neighbouring and opposite condition.
questions.trick: Zero shear → maximum moment. Zero moment → contraflexure.
questions.mn: Contraflexure: the beam changes its mind.

questions.q: The overall efficiency of a hydropower plant is the product of the:
o: Turbine efficiency and the generator efficiency
Turbine efficiency and the hydraulic efficiency only
Generator efficiency and the transmission efficiency only
Volumetric efficiency and the mechanical efficiency only
questions.s: Overall efficiency is the ratio of electrical output to the water power available, so it combines what the turbine converts with what the generator delivers.
questions.trap: Hydraulic, volumetric and mechanical efficiencies are all stages *inside* the turbine efficiency, so quoting them again double-counts.
questions.trick: Follow the energy: water to shaft is the turbine, shaft to wire is the generator.
